                   G6 LANDOWNERS LEGAL FUND INITIAL BRIEF

       COMES NOW, The G6 Landowners Legal Fund, LLC (“G6 Landowners”), and files this

its Initial Brief to address the factors needed by the Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) and the

Public Utility Commission of Texas (the “Commission”) in identifying the route that best meets

the statutory and regulatory requirements applicable to this proceeding. The evidentiary record

demonstrates that no route utilizing the G6 Link satisfies those factors, and that Route 894, as

proposed by the Applicants, best complies with the statutory and regulatory factors that govern

this proceeding and should be recommended by the ALJs and adopted by the Commission.

       This Initial Brief provides an analysis of the factors required to be considered by the

Commission in making its routing decision in the context of the community and properties that

would be affected by the G6 Link, drawn from the direct testimonies filed by G6 Landowners’

members, as well as that filed by Janet L. Rose, individually and as Trustee of the Joppa 1886

Trust. The Brief then demonstrates the basis for the ALJs proposing and the Commission adopting
                                                   1
 Route 894 as the route that best complies with those factors; and discusses evidence in the record

illustrating why other routes advocated by Intervenors in this proceeding do not best meet the

applicable factors.

       The Applicants, based on information that was available to them, have correctly

determined that Route 894, which does not utilize the G6 Link, is the “best meets” route for this

proceeding. There is additional evidence in the record that bolsters that decision not to utilize the

G6 Link. The basis for selecting Route 894 is fully supported by the record. The record also

demonstrates that other routes proposed by other Intervenors are inferior to Route 894. G6

Landowners respectfully requests that the Administrative Law Judges propose and the

Commission adopt Route 894 as the “best meets” route for this proceeding.

       G6 Landowners shows as follows:

        I. PUC FACTOR ANALYSIS AND THE G6 CORRIDOR: OVERVIEW OF
                  AFFECTED COMMUNITIES AND PROPERTIES

       In making its routing decision, the Commission is required to base its decision on the

factors set forth in PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B). Those factors

include a consideration of community values; recreational and park areas; historical and aesthetic

values; environmental integrity; engineering constraints; and cost. The factors also include

whether the routes parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way for electric facilities;

whether the routes parallel or utilize other existing compatible rights-of-way, including roads,

highways, railroads, or telephone utility rights-of-way; whether the routes parallel property lines

or other natural or cultural features; and whether the routes conform with the policy of prudent

avoidance.

       The Applicants’ Table 7-3 data provide the objective baseline against which the G6 Link

is evaluated in this section. Those quantified measurements, reported for each link in the

                                                 2
 Application, are the same data that G6 Landowners’ expert, Ryan Hopkins, used as the exclusive

inputs to his independent composite scoring analysis of all 123 routes evaluated in this proceeding.

Mr. Hopkins also provided a qualitative analysis of the G6 Link based on the testimony of G6 Link

landowners.

       The G6 Link, as proposed by Applicants, would traverse a continuous corridor of rural

Burnet County land that is neither vacant nor generic open space. It is land in active,

multigenerational residential, agricultural, recreational, and conservation use; land defined by the

North Fork of the San Gabriel River and its tributaries, and by the families who have stewarded it

for generations. The evidence regarding the G6 Link, drawn from the direct testimonies of eleven

G6 Landowners members, Mr. Hopkins, and Janet Rose documents a pattern of overlapping and

compounding impacts across every statutory factor the Commission is required to consider.

       In support of his testimony, Mr. Hopkins prepared and submitted into evidence two map

books: a Floodplain Map Book and a Wetlands Map Book, comprising twenty-four sheets each

that span the full length of the G6 corridor and overlay publicly available federal data, including

FEMA flood hazard designations and USFWS National Wetlands Inventory features, onto the

proposed alignment. Those map books are referenced throughout this section.

       Amelia Sarot additionally submitted ten aerial drone video recordings, captured May 11-

12, 2026, depicting the terrain, vegetation, waterways, habitable structures, agricultural

improvements, and rural character of the proposed G6 corridor as it exists today, flying as close to

the proposed centerline as safely and legally practicable. The recordings cover those properties

along the G6 corridor to which Ms. Sarot had lawful access and do not represent the full length of

the link; they are offered as a fair and accurate visual representation of the portions of the corridor

they depict, not as a complete survey of the route. Those recordings are in evidence as Exhibits A

 through J of Ms. Sarot’s direct testimony and are referenced throughout this section of the Initial

Brief where relevant to specific properties and features depicted in the footage. These recordings

provide a broader view of the characteristics of the properties along the G6 Link and demonstrate

the impacts that would be suffered if a route using the G6 Link is chosen as the “best meets” route

in this proceeding.1

        A. Habitable Structures and Land Use – Prudent Avoidance

        Applicants' characterization of the G6 corridor as “rural” or “open” land does not

accurately reflect the active and continuous human use of the affected parcels. The Applicants'

land use data tells the story plainly: of the 16.16 miles comprising the G6 Link, 12.31 miles cross

rangeland pasture and an additional 0.68 miles cross cropland and hay meadow, meaning that more

than 80 % of the link traverses active agricultural land.2

        The record confirms what those numbers reflect on the ground. Many intervening

landowners traversed by the link, including Wilson, Powell, Duckworth, Rutledge, Moldenhauer,

Ellett, Busby, Wallace, Perez, and Rose, operate active cattle operations, either directly or through

a cattle lease, as do many of the adjacent members personally visited by Ms. Sarot, including

Brock, Chaney, Edwards, Hetherly, and Logan. 3 This is not open space. It is working Texas ranch

land, and it has been for generations.

        Additionally, as Mr. Hopkins testified, at least 11 of the 24 mapping sheets depict habitable

residential structures within the 500-foot prudent-avoidance setback envelope of the proposed

centerline.4 The G6 Link’s habitable structure profile is inconsistent with the Commission’s policy

of prudent avoidance where, as here, reasonable alternatives exist that avoid those impacts with no

        B. Compatible Rights-of-Way

        The Commission’s rules direct that, to the extent reasonable, a proposed transmission line

should parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way (“ROW”), including electric

transmission lines, railroads, pipelines, highways, and should parallel property lines or other

natural or cultural features. 24 These are related but distinct concepts. Co-location with an existing

utility, transportation, or pipeline right-of-way places a new line within a corridor that has already

been disturbed, reducing new land-use impact. Paralleling a property boundary, by contrast, does

not require any existing infrastructure at all; it simply means the route tracks a legal boundary line,

which may run through entirely undisturbed land on both sides. The rule's preference for

compatible rights-of-way is aimed primarily at the former.

        The Applicants' data shows that the G6 Link achieves no true ROW co-location. Of the G6

Link’s 16.16 total miles, the link runs parallel to zero miles of existing electric transmission lines,

zero pipelines, zero miles of railroads, and zero miles of existing public roads or highways. 25 The

entire 16.16-mile length of the G6 Link establishes a new industrial corridor with no co-location

with previously disturbed transmission, transportation, or pipeline infrastructure for any sustained

distance.

             The Application states that the link does parallel apparent property boundaries for 5.44 of

limited routing preference for property-boundary parallelism. A review of the Applicants’ route

maps cross-referenced against Attachment 12 - PUC Mailing List, Bell County - Big Hill, shows

that several of the segments likely counted as boundary-paralleling run along what appears on the

map to be a property line but is, in fact, an interior division between multiple platted parcels held

by a single landowner. Ammie Busby owns Tract 2066 and is a part owner of the adjacent Tract

2067, meaning the route’s apparent paralleling between those two tracts is actually paralleling

within a single ownership interest rather than a true boundary between separate landowners.

Similarly, Bill Price owns, to varying degrees, Tracts 2072, 2073, 2074, 2075, 2076, 2077, and

2079, and the route’s apparent boundary-paralleling across that cluster of tracts is, in substance, a

path through the interior of one contiguous holding rather than along the edge of distinct properties.

Link-wide, the G6 Link traverses 43 parcels held by 24 distinct landowner profiles (accounting for

joint ownership by spouses, family groups, and entities), and of those 24 profiles, only eight are

traversed along an actual property line; the remaining 16 have their properties directly and

substantially split by the G6 alignment running through the interior of their land, not along the

edge.26

Assessment states that the property boundary maps used to locate apparent property boundaries

consisted of GIS data from county tax offices and appraisal districts, not from any consolidation

of parcels by common ownership.27 Because appraisal district parcel data reflects platted tax lots

rather than ownership groupings, the Applicants’ apparent-property-boundary figure cannot

with these limitations in mind. The practical consequence is that any route incorporating the G6

Link forfeits the land-use efficiency the Commission’s rules are designed to promote.

           C. Environmental Integrity

           PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(D) requires the Commission to consider environmental integrity in

evaluating a proposed route, and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) directs that this consideration include

the route’s impact on riparian areas, wetlands, surface water, and habitat. The Applicants’ Table

7-3 data, measured link by link across the same categories applied throughout this Application,

provides the baseline against which the G6 Link’s environmental impact is evaluated.

Branch, Campbell’s Creek, and Olive Branch, are the primary surface water features of this

segment of Burnet County. The river corridor anchors the daily lives, water supply, and land use

of many properties along the G6 corridor. The application data directly shows this, as it notes that

the G6 Link crosses water far more frequently, and disturbs far more sensitive terrain, than its

length alone would suggest. The link records 31 stream crossings across its 16.16 miles, meaning

the route crosses a stream on average nearly every half mile of its length. 29 The G6 Link crosses

        B. Compatible Rights-of-Way

        The Commission's rules direct that, to the extent reasonable, a proposed transmission line

should parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way ("ROW"), including electric

transmission lines, railroads, pipelines, highways, and should parallel property lines or other

natural or cultural features.24 These are related but distinct concepts. Co-location with an existing

utility, transportation, or pipeline right-of-way places a new line within a corridor that has already

been disturbed, reducing new land-use impact. Paralleling a property boundary, by contrast, does

not require any existing infrastructure at all; it simply means the route tracks a legal boundary line,

which may run through entirely undisturbed land on both sides. The rule's preference for

compatible rights-of-way is aimed primarily at the former.

        The Applicants' data shows that the G6 Link achieves no true ROW co-location. Of the G6

Link's 16.16 total miles, the link runs parallel to zero miles of existing electric transmission lines,

zero pipelines, zero miles of railroads, and zero miles of existing public roads or highways.25 The

entire 16.16-mile length of the G6 Link establishes a new industrial corridor with no co-location

with previously disturbed transmission, transportation, or pipeline infrastructure for any sustained

distance.
